front_blocks.md: Define **development**.

back_blocks.md: **Development** is a country's positive progress in improving the **standard of living** and **quality of life** for its population.

cards.front_md: Define **development**.
cards.back_md: **Development** is a country's positive progress in improving the **standard of living** and **quality of life** for its population.

front_blocks.md: Why is it better to use **multiple indicators** to measure development?

back_blocks.md: Individual indicators are **misleading** alone because some features develop before others; using multiple indicators produces a **clearer picture** of a country's development.

cards.front_md: Why is it better to use **multiple indicators** to measure development?
cards.back_md: Individual indicators are **misleading** alone because some features develop before others; using multiple indicators produces a **clearer picture** of a country's development.

front_blocks.md: Define **GDP per capita**.

back_blocks.md: **GDP per capita** is the total value of **goods and services produced within a country** in a year, **divided by its population**.

cards.front_md: Define **GDP per capita**.
cards.back_md: **GDP per capita** is the total value of **goods and services produced within a country** in a year, **divided by its population**.

front_blocks.md: Why can **GDP per capita** be a misleading measure of development?

back_blocks.md: It is an **average**, so variation in wealth is **hidden**, and there is no way of knowing what the GDP is spent on (e.g. it rises after an earthquake due to rebuilding).

cards.front_md: Why can **GDP per capita** be a misleading measure of development?
cards.back_md: It is an **average**, so variation in wealth is **hidden**, and there is no way of knowing what the GDP is spent on (e.g. it rises after an earthquake due to rebuilding).

front_blocks.md: What is **Purchasing Power Parity (PPP)** used to adjust for?

back_blocks.md: It adjusts **GNP per capita** for the **cost of living**, since \$1 goes further in Bangladesh than in the USA.

cards.front_md: What is **Purchasing Power Parity (PPP)** used to adjust for?
cards.back_md: It adjusts **GNP per capita** for the **cost of living**, since \$1 goes further in Bangladesh than in the USA.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
GNI is calculated by adding a country's income from foreign sources to its GDP.

back_blocks.md: **True.** **GNI** is found by adding a country's income from foreign sources (like remittances and investment income) to its **GDP**.

cards.front_md:
**True or False?**

GNI is calculated by adding a country's income from foreign sources to its GDP.
cards.back_md: **True.** **GNI** is found by adding a country's income from foreign sources (like remittances and investment income) to its **GDP**.

front_blocks.md: Which organisation now uses **GNI** more commonly than GDP?

back_blocks.md: The **World Bank**; the **European Union** also uses it to determine each member country's contribution.

cards.front_md: Which organisation now uses **GNI** more commonly than GDP?
cards.back_md: The **World Bank**; the **European Union** also uses it to determine each member country's contribution.

front_blocks.md: What is the key difference between **GNI** and **GNI per capita**?

back_blocks.md: **GNI** measures a country's **overall economic wealth**, while **GNI per capita** (GNI divided by population) shows the **average income / standard of living** per person.

cards.front_md: What is the key difference between **GNI** and **GNI per capita**?
cards.back_md: **GNI** measures a country's **overall economic wealth**, while **GNI per capita** (GNI divided by population) shows the **average income / standard of living** per person.

front_blocks.md: Define the **infant mortality rate**.

back_blocks.md: The **infant mortality rate** is the number of children per **1000** who die below the age of **1**.

cards.front_md: Define the **infant mortality rate**.
cards.back_md: The **infant mortality rate** is the number of children per **1000** who die below the age of **1**.

front_blocks.md: Define the **literacy rate**.

back_blocks.md: The **literacy rate** is the percentage of people over **15 years old** who can **read and write**.

cards.front_md: Define the **literacy rate**.
cards.back_md: The **literacy rate** is the percentage of people over **15 years old** who can **read and write**.

front_blocks.md: In developed countries, literacy rates average around 96%, whereas in less-developed countries they average around **______** per cent.

back_blocks.md: In developed countries, literacy rates average around 96%, whereas in less-developed countries they average around **65** per cent.

cards.front_md: In developed countries, literacy rates average around 96%, whereas in less-developed countries they average around **______** per cent.
cards.back_md: In developed countries, literacy rates average around 96%, whereas in less-developed countries they average around **65** per cent.

front_blocks.md: Why does a **lower 'people per doctor'** figure usually indicate greater development?

back_blocks.md: It means there are **more doctors per person**, which usually reflects a **stronger healthcare system**.

cards.front_md: Why does a **lower 'people per doctor'** figure usually indicate greater development?
cards.back_md: It means there are **more doctors per person**, which usually reflects a **stronger healthcare system**.

front_blocks.md: Why is **calorie intake** used as a development indicator?

back_blocks.md: It reflects a country's overall **economic and food security status**; developed countries tend to have a higher average daily calorie intake than less developed ones.

cards.front_md: Why is **calorie intake** used as a development indicator?
cards.back_md: It reflects a country's overall **economic and food security status**; developed countries tend to have a higher average daily calorie intake than less developed ones.

front_blocks.md: What do **social** development indicators reveal that economic ones do not?

back_blocks.md: They give a more complete picture of **how a country's money helps its people**, covering quality of life, equal opportunities, access to education and healthcare, life expectancy and education levels.

cards.front_md: What do **social** development indicators reveal that economic ones do not?
cards.back_md: They give a more complete picture of **how a country's money helps its people**, covering quality of life, equal opportunities, access to education and healthcare, life expectancy and education levels.

front_blocks.md: Give two examples of **economic** development indicators.

back_blocks.md: **Employment, income and wealth**; savings, house building and consumer spending; international **trade**; and resources with pollution controls.

cards.front_md: Give two examples of **economic** development indicators.
cards.back_md: **Employment, income and wealth**; savings, house building and consumer spending; international **trade**; and resources with pollution controls.

front_blocks.md: Individual indicators are misleading when used alone, so using **______** indicators provides a clearer picture of a country's development.

back_blocks.md: Individual indicators are misleading when used alone, so using **multiple** indicators provides a clearer picture of a country's development.

cards.front_md: Individual indicators are misleading when used alone, so using **______** indicators provides a clearer picture of a country's development.
cards.back_md: Individual indicators are misleading when used alone, so using **multiple** indicators provides a clearer picture of a country's development.

front_blocks.md: Why is **GNI** limited as a development indicator?

back_blocks.md: It only measures **income**; it is an **average** that a few wealthy people can distort, income data is sensitive so may be dishonest, and **informal-sector workers and stay-at-home parents** are not counted.

cards.front_md: Why is **GNI** limited as a development indicator?
cards.back_md: It only measures **income**; it is an **average** that a few wealthy people can distort, income data is sensitive so may be dishonest, and **informal-sector workers and stay-at-home parents** are not counted.

front_blocks.md: Why can **life expectancy** be misleading in countries with high infant mortality?

back_blocks.md: People who **survive infancy** may live longer than expected, so the figure can be distorted; data is also often unreliable in LICs.

cards.front_md: Why can **life expectancy** be misleading in countries with high infant mortality?
cards.back_md: People who **survive infancy** may live longer than expected, so the figure can be distorted; data is also often unreliable in LICs.

front_blocks.md: Why is **death rate** a less reliable development measure than birth rate?

back_blocks.md: Death rates can be high in LICs due to **poverty** but also high in HICs where many people die of **old age**, so it does not clearly reflect development.

cards.front_md: Why is **death rate** a less reliable development measure than birth rate?
cards.back_md: Death rates can be high in LICs due to **poverty** but also high in HICs where many people die of **old age**, so it does not clearly reflect development.

front_blocks.md: Why might official figures for **access to safe water** underestimate the problem?

back_blocks.md: Data collection in LICs is often inaccurate; people may technically have access but **high costs** force them to use unsafe water, and leaking pipes or natural disasters can cut supply.

cards.front_md: Why might official figures for **access to safe water** underestimate the problem?
cards.back_md: Data collection in LICs is often inaccurate; people may technically have access but **high costs** force them to use unsafe water, and leaking pipes or natural disasters can cut supply.

front_blocks.md: What is the **Human Development Index (HDI)**, and who created it?

back_blocks.md: The **HDI** is a combined measure of development created by the **UN in 1990**, scored from **0 to 1**; a higher score means higher development and quality of life.

cards.front_md: What is the **Human Development Index (HDI)**, and who created it?
cards.back_md: The **HDI** is a combined measure of development created by the **UN in 1990**, scored from **0 to 1**; a higher score means higher development and quality of life.

front_blocks.md: Which **four indicators** make up the HDI?

back_blocks.md: **Life expectancy at birth**, **mean years of schooling** (adults aged 25), **expected years of schooling**, and **GNI per capita (PPP\$)**.

cards.front_md: Which **four indicators** make up the HDI?
cards.back_md: **Life expectancy at birth**, **mean years of schooling** (adults aged 25), **expected years of schooling**, and **GNI per capita (PPP\$)**.

front_blocks.md: In 2024, Norway had the highest HDI at 0.957, while **______** had the lowest at 0.394.

back_blocks.md: In 2024, Norway had the highest HDI at 0.957, while **Niger** had the lowest at 0.394.

cards.front_md: In 2024, Norway had the highest HDI at 0.957, while **______** had the lowest at 0.394.
cards.back_md: In 2024, Norway had the highest HDI at 0.957, while **Niger** had the lowest at 0.394.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
The HDI takes environmental and political factors into account.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
The HDI uses only **four indicators** and does **not** take into account environmental or political measures, or disparities within a country.

back_blocks.md: **Very High**, **High**, **Medium**, and **Low** Human Development.
